content:
Hello,

It's my hope that this proves useful to folks here. I appreciate any Good / Bad / Ugly feedback in any case.

I've attempted formalization of two classical facts about Lehmer's polynomial
L(x) = x^10 + x^9 − x^7 − x^6 − x^5 − x^4 − x^3 + x + 1 in Lean 4 / Mathlib:

  1. L is irreducible over ℤ, and
  2. the characteristic polynomial of a Coxeter element of the E₁₀ Weyl group is L
    (the rank-10 case of McMullen, *Coxeter groups, Salem numbers and the Hilbert
    metric*, Publ. Math. IHÉS 95 (2002)).

Repo: https://github.com/dillon-11/lehmer-E10

The claim is stated in a single Challenge.lean importing only Mathlib — it defines
L, the E₁₀ generalized Cartan matrix, the simple reflections on the root lattice,
and the Coxeter element as the product s₀s₁⋯s₉, ending in

theorem main_theorem :
    Irreducible lehmerPolynomial ∧ coxeterE10.charpoly = lehmerPolynomial

Verification without reading the proof: comparator is set up (config.json at
the repo root, commands in the README); it confirms that main_theorem in the proof
library proves exactly the Challenge.lean statement, uses only
propext/Classical.choice/Quot.sound, and passes kernel replay. A filled-in
formalization.yaml is at the root. Toolchain v4.32.0-rc1.

Proof route, briefly: L is reciprocal, so its roots pair through the trace
y = z + 1/z, which satisfies the quintic q(y) = y⁵ + y⁴ − 5y³ − 5y² + 4y + 3.
IVT sign checks place four roots of q in (−2,2) (giving eight roots of L on
the unit circle) and one in (2, 21/10) (the Salem pair {μ, 1/μ} off it). A
proper monic factorization L = F·G forces |F(0)| = μᵃ(1/μ)ᵇ = 1 with
a,b ∈ {0,1}, and all four cases die — the all-on-circle cases via Kronecker's
1857 theorem (proved here in root form from Mathlib's
NumberField.Embeddings.pow_eq_one_of_norm_eq_one) plus the fact that no
cyclotomic polynomial divides L, which has a pleasant uniform proof: L(2) = 1291
is prime and 2 is a primitive root mod 1291, so Φ_k ∣ L would force
1290 ∣ k, i.e. φ(k) ≥ 336 > 10. The charpoly identity then follows from a
kernel-checked evaluation of the reflection product and L(C) = 0 via
Cayley–Hamilton and minimal-polynomial divisibility.

Two things that might be independently useful:

  • kronecker_roots (Kronecker's theorem, root form) — I didn't find it in Mathlib;
    happy to attempt a PR if there's interest.

  • the uniform cyclotomic-divisor kill via a single prime witness, which seems like
    a reusable trick for concrete irreducibility proofs.

A small follow-up to this thread: I've published a second repo produced by the
same pipeline as lehmer-e10, plus a short note on the pipeline itself, in case
the method is useful to anyone working on explicit/analytic statements.
Repo 2: hl-twins — *the Hardy–Littlewood twin asymptotic implies the
twin prime conjecture*, as one fully discharged main_theorem:

if twinCount x satisfies the ε-form asymptotic
twinCount x ~ 2·C₂ · x/(log x)², then there are infinitely many twin
primes

where everything (I presume) that makes this non-circular is:

  • 0 < 2·C₂ — positivity of the restricted product 2·∏(1 − 1/(p−1)²),
    via log-summability of the defects;

  • x/(log x)² → ∞ — divergence of the main term;

  • the partial-summation transfer — the classical step from the
    Λ-weighted form Σ_{n<X} Λ(n)Λ(n+2) ~ S(2)·X down to the unweighted
    count. This is the largest proof in the set: the Λ-sum differs from the
    twin-weighted sum by a prime-power contribution of size O(√X·(log X)³)
    (proper prime powers inject into (minFac, exponent) pairs), and a
    Chebyshev-style cut at Y = ⌊x^(1−δ)⌋ converts the weighted asymptotic
    into the count asymptotic. So tpc_of_hardyLittlewoodLambda: the Λ-form
    Hardy–Littlewood asymptotic alone implies infinitude, with no auxiliary
    hypotheses.

There's also a place-by-place account of the singular series in the Λ-form
module: S(2) = 2·C₂ exactly, and odd shifts vanish because parity forces
one member of any Λ-supported pair onto the powers of 2
(odd_shift_dyadic). Supporting structure lemmas (every twin pair past
(3,5) is (6k−1, 6k+1), the mod-4 chirality split, 5 as the only prime in
two twin pairs) are included with doc comments. The remaining conjectural
input is a plain Prop definition taken as a hypothesis — the repo contains
no axioms and no sorries outside Challenge.lean; #print axioms on
every declaration shows only [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound].

A procedural note: the transfer was first stated as an interface Prop and only
later proven — and the proof slotted in without restating or touching
anything downstream. Some lemmas may be independently reusable
(properPrimePow_card_le, positivity of ∏(1 − aₚ) from summable defects,
(log x)ⁿ/x^r → 0).

The pipeline (same one that produced lehmer-e10), for what it's worth:

  1. Candidate statements are tested numerically before formalization, and
    every numerical test ships with a mutation control — the test must fail
    on deliberately corrupted input before the result is accepted. This has
    caught real artifacts (boundary bugs, generally).

  2. Constants enter Lean only through interval certification (MPFR interval
    arithmetic against high-precision data), never as floats read off a
    computation. (Not exercised in in this instance, which is currently constant-free)

  3. **External published theorems enter as single named axioms with printed
    bills** — never as silent sorrys — so #print axioms shows exactly what
    is imported and from where. (Also not needed here: this repo is
    foundational-only.)

  4. Audit gates: build green; comment-stripped
    scan for sorry/axiom; doc-comment coverage for every public theorem;
    the #print axioms output checked against a whitelist.

I'd genuinely welcome criticism of the statement packaging in particular —
stating conjectural inputs as hypothesis Props (HardyLittlewoodTwin,
etc.) with the discharge theorems proven downstream. Additionally, anything that could make any of this more useful in terms of approach, typing, structure that I have failed to capture already would be good to know so that I may improve upon this somewhat quixotic exercise of approaching opaque topics through an opaque LLM medium.

repo: https://github.com/dillon-11/hl-twins · audit + build instructions in the README
